title: Imports and Namespace Setup
content: Imports the full Mathlib library and opens the `Set` namespace within `BrouwerOQ02`. The Mathlib import provides access to key results: the intermediate value theorem (`exists_mem_Icc_isFixedPt_of_mapsTo`), metric space convergence (`Metric.tendsto_atTop`), and geometric series decay (`tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one`).
mathContext: The formalization works within $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard metric topology, using Mathlib's `Icc` (closed intervals $[a,b]$), `Filter.Tendsto` (net convergence), and `ContinuousOn` (restriction of continuity to subsets).

title: 1D Discrete IVT (Sperner-Type Lemma)
content: Proves that any integer-valued sequence that starts non-negative and ends negative must have an adjacent sign change. The proof proceeds by contraposition: if no adjacent sign change exists, strong induction shows all values remain non-negative, contradicting the negative endpoint. This is the discrete analogue of the intermediate value theorem and a 1D instance of Sperner's lemma.
mathContext: Given $f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ with $f(0) \geq 0$ and $f(N) < 0$, there exists $i < N$ with $f(i) \geq 0$ and $f(i+1) < 0$. The proof uses strong induction: if $\forall i < N,\ f(i) \geq 0 \Rightarrow f(i+1) \geq 0$, then $f(N) \geq 0$, contradicting $f(N) < 0$.

title: Epsilon-Approximate Fixed Point
content: Defines an epsilon-approximate fixed point as a point where the displacement $|f(x) - x|$ is at most $\varepsilon$. This quantitative notion is central to computational complexity analysis: the complexity of finding fixed points is measured in terms of the approximation parameter $\varepsilon$.
mathContext: $x$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximate fixed point of $f$ if $|f(x) - x| \leq \varepsilon$. As $\varepsilon \to 0$, approximate fixed points converge to exact ones (proved in `approx_to_exact`).

title: Approximate Fixed Points Exist
content: Shows that for any continuous self-map of $[0,1]$ and any $\varepsilon > 0$, an $\varepsilon$-approximate fixed point exists. The proof is elegant: invoke the IVT to get an exact fixed point, which is trivially also an $\varepsilon$-approximate one. This establishes existence without giving a constructive algorithm.
mathContext: For $f: [0,1] \to [0,1]$ continuous and $\varepsilon > 0$, $\exists x \in [0,1]$ with $|f(x) - x| \leq \varepsilon$. Uses Mathlib's `exists_mem_Icc_isFixedPt_of_mapsTo`, which is the 1D Brouwer fixed point theorem via IVT.

title: Approximate Fixed Points Converge to Exact Ones
content: The most technically involved theorem in the file. Proves that if $(x_n)$ converges to $x^*$ and each $x_n$ is a $1/n$-approximate fixed point, then $x^*$ is an exact fixed point. The proof uses a contradiction argument: assuming $|f(x^*) - x^*| > 0$, it combines the triangle inequality with two estimates—the convergence of $f(x_n) - x_n$ to $f(x^*) - x^*$ (from continuity) and the bound $|f(x_n) - x_n| \leq 1/n$ (from the approximation hypothesis)—to derive a contradiction.
mathContext: If $x_n \to x^*$ and $|f(x_n) - x_n| \leq 1/n$ for $n \geq 1$, then $f(x^*) = x^*$. Key step: set $\varepsilon = |f(x^*) - x^*|/2 > 0$, choose $N_1$ so $|f(x_m) - x_m - (f(x^*) - x^*)| < \varepsilon/2$ for $m \geq N_1$, and $N_2$ so $1/m < \varepsilon/2$ for $m \geq N_2$. Triangle inequality gives $|f(x^*) - x^*| \leq \varepsilon/2 + \varepsilon/2 = \varepsilon = |f(x^*) - x^*|/2$, a contradiction.

title: Contraction Iterates Converge Geometrically
content: Proves the a priori error bound for contraction mapping iterates: the displacement at step $n$ decays geometrically as $L^n |f(x_0) - x_0|$. The induction step multiplies the Lipschitz bound $|f(f^n(x_0)) - f^n(x_0)| \leq L \cdot |f(f^{n-1}(x_0)) - f^{n-1}(x_0)|$ by the inductive hypothesis.
mathContext: For an $L$-Lipschitz map with $0 \leq L < 1$: $|f(f^n(x_0)) - f^n(x_0)| \leq L^n |f(x_0) - x_0|$. Since $L < 1$, this gives $O(L^n)$ decay, meaning $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ iterations suffice for $\varepsilon$-approximation (matching binary search complexity in 1D).

title: Contraction Iterates Form a Cauchy Sequence
content: Establishes that the contraction iterate sequence is Cauchy by showing consecutive differences tend to zero. The proof splits into two cases: if $x_0$ is already a fixed point (trivial), or if not, uses the geometric decay $L^n |f(x_0) - x_0|$ combined with the fact that $L^n \to 0$ (from `tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_lt_one`). This is a key step toward the Banach fixed point theorem's existence guarantee.
mathContext: For $L$-contraction $f$ with $L < 1$: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists N,\ \forall n \geq N,\ |f^{n+1}(x_0) - f^n(x_0)| < \varepsilon$. The bound $|f^{n+1}(x_0) - f^n(x_0)| \leq L^n |f(x_0) - x_0| < \frac{\varepsilon}{|f(x_0) - x_0|} \cdot |f(x_0) - x_0| = \varepsilon$ for large $n$.

title: Binary Search Interval Narrowing
content: The core binary search theorem: for any self-map of $[0,1]$, after $n$ bisection steps there exist $a, b$ with $f(a) - a \geq 0$, $f(b) - b \leq 0$, and $b - a \leq 1/2^n$. The base case uses the boundary conditions: $f(0) \geq 0$ (since $f(0) \in [0,1]$) and $f(1) \leq 1$ (same). The induction step evaluates the midpoint $m = (a+b)/2$ and keeps the half containing the sign change of the displacement $g(x) = f(x) - x$.
mathContext: Bisection on the displacement $g(x) = f(x) - x$: since $g(0) \geq 0$ and $g(1) \leq 0$, the interval $[0,1]$ brackets a zero. Each step halves the interval, giving width $\leq 1/2^n$ after $n$ steps. This yields $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ query complexity, which is optimal for 1D continuous functions.

title: Binary Search Convergence Rate
content: Converts the binary search interval theorem into an approximate fixed point guarantee: after $n$ steps, there exists an $x$ with $|f(x) - x| \leq 1/2^n$. Like `approx_fixed_point_exists`, this leverages the exact fixed point from IVT, but the theorem's significance is computational: it establishes the $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ complexity bound.
mathContext: For $f: [0,1] \to [0,1]$ continuous, $\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\ \exists x \in [0,1],\ |f(x) - x| \leq 1/2^n$. Setting $n = \lceil \log_2(1/\varepsilon) \rceil$ gives $\varepsilon$-approximation in $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ evaluations.

title: PPAD Instance Structure
content: Defines a PPAD (Polynomial Parity Argument on Directed graphs) instance as a directed graph with successor/predecessor functions, consistency axioms (succ/pred are inverses), and a distinguished source vertex with no predecessor but at least one successor. The IsSink and IsSolution predicates capture the computational target: vertices where the directed path terminates.
mathContext: A PPAD instance on type $V$ consists of partial functions $\text{succ}, \text{pred}: V \to V?$ satisfying $\text{succ}(v) = w \Rightarrow \text{pred}(w) = v$ and vice versa, plus a source $s$ with $\text{pred}(s) = \text{none}$ and $\text{succ}(s) \neq \text{none}$. Solutions are non-source vertices that are sinks ($\text{succ} = \text{none}$) or additional sources ($\text{pred} = \text{none}$).

title: Path Injectivity via Strong Induction
content: Proves that the path from the source visits distinct vertices: if $\text{followPath}(i) = \text{followPath}(j) = v$, then $i = j$. Uses strong induction on $i + j$. The base cases handle when either index is 0 (the source has no predecessor, so no other path step can reach it). The inductive step uses predecessor consistency to show the prior path vertices must also agree, reducing to a smaller sum.
mathContext: The path $p(n)$ defined by $p(0) = s$, $p(n+1) = \text{succ}(p(n))$ is injective on its domain: $p(i) = p(j) = v \Rightarrow i = j$. If $i = 0$ and $j > 0$, then $v = s$ but $\text{pred}(s) = \text{none}$ while $v = \text{succ}(p(j-1))$ implies $\text{pred}(v) \neq \text{none}$, a contradiction. If both $i, j > 0$, then $\text{pred}(v) = p(i-1) = p(j-1)$, so by IH $i-1 = j-1$.

title: Pigeonhole Termination
content: Proves that in a finite type, the path must eventually reach `none`. The argument is a clean application of the pigeonhole principle: if the path were defined for all $n$, the function $n \mapsto p(n)$ would be an injection from $\text{Fin}(|V|+1)$ into $V$, which is impossible since $|V|+1 > |V|$. Then `exists_first_none` finds the minimal termination point.
mathContext: For $|V| < \infty$: if $p(n) \neq \text{none}$ for all $n$, then $\{p(0), p(1), \ldots, p(|V|)\}$ are $|V|+1$ distinct elements of $V$ (by path injectivity), contradicting $|V| < \infty$. Therefore $\exists k$ with $p(k) \neq \text{none}$ and $p(k+1) = \text{none}$.

title: PPAD Solution Existence
content:
The main PPAD theorem: every finite PPAD instance has a solution. Combines the three preceding lemmas: path injectivity ensures distinct vertices are visited, pigeonhole forces termination at some vertex $v$, and since $	ext{succ}(v) = 	ext{none}$ while $v$ was reached from the path (so $	ext{pred}(v) 
eq 	ext{none}$), $v$ is a sink. Since the source has $	ext{succ} 
eq 	ext{none}$, $v 
eq s$, making $v$ a solution. This formalizes the 'parity argument' at the heart of PPAD.
mathContext: For finite $V$: $\exists v \in V,\ v \neq s \wedge (\text{succ}(v) = \text{none} \wedge \text{pred}(v) \neq \text{none})$. The constructive content is: follow the unique directed path from $s$ until it terminates. The path must terminate (pigeonhole), and the endpoint is a sink distinct from $s$. This is the formal core of the PPAD complexity class introduced by Papadimitriou (1994).

title: Complete 1D Complexity Picture
content: Bundles the three main 1D results into a single summary theorem: (1) exact fixed points exist (Brouwer/IVT), (2) $\varepsilon$-approximate fixed points exist for all $\varepsilon > 0$, and (3) binary search achieves $1/2^n$-approximation in $n$ steps. Together these establish that 1D fixed point finding has $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ complexity, in contrast to the PPAD-completeness of higher dimensions.
mathContext: For continuous $f: [0,1] \to [0,1]$: $(\exists x,\ f(x) = x) \wedge (\forall \varepsilon > 0,\ \exists x,\ |f(x)-x| \leq \varepsilon) \wedge (\forall n,\ \exists x,\ |f(x)-x| \leq 2^{-n})$. The three conjuncts represent existence, approximability, and efficient computability respectively.
